title: Teach For America was once a movement. What happened? https://fordhaminstitute.org/national/commentary/teach-america-was-once-movement-what-happened
author: Dale Chu
source: The Thomas B. Fordham Institute (fordhaminstitute.org), September 24, 2026
summary: Writing for Fordham's Flypaper on Teach For America's 35th anniversary, TFA alumnus Dale Chu asks how an organization that once built a bipartisan talent pipeline lost its way. He takes Doug Lemov's stinging verdict that TFA traded a focus on student achievement for political objectives as his starting point. Chu recalls his own 1997 corps as left-leaning but deliberately nonpolitical, united by the simple pitch to teach poor children who deserved a great education. He traces the decline to two forces: a changed culture and labor market that shrank the corps from about 6,000 in 2013 to roughly 1,600 in 2022, and a self-inflicted shift that moved politics from the background to the brand. Because the newer message asked recruits to agree on contested questions about injustice, the big tent narrowed. Chu ends cautiously hopeful that new CEO Aneesh Sohoni's emphasis on reading, math, and readiness could restore the organization's original focus.
points: TFA's founding idea was a human capital play: compete with Wall Street and consulting firms for top graduates and send them to hard-to-staff schools.
Its early power came from not making politics a condition of belonging, letting people of different views rally around one mission.
Applications peaked at 57,000 with nearly 6,000 new corps members in 2013, but the incoming corps fell to about 1,600 by 2022.
As its pitch morphed into joining a broader struggle against systemic injustice, TFA required agreement on contested questions and lost its big tent.
Chu sees an opening for renewal as disappointing achievement results return attention to the basic work of schools.
quotes: It produced not only achievement gains among students taught by TFA corps members, but also an elite talent pipeline, as alumni went on to leadership roles across business, medicine, law, and other fields, while many remained in education.

But the original idea behind TFA was fundamentally about human capital. Compete directly with Wall Street investment firms and management consultancies for high-achieving undergraduates, then place them in inner-city schools that struggled to attract teachers.

When I joined the corps in 1997, Teach For America was hardly a conservative outfit. Most of my fellow corps members leaned left. But importantly, TFA seemed determined not to make politics a condition of belonging.
At its peak in 2013, TFA drew 57,000 applicants and nearly 6,000 new corps members. By 2022, the incoming corps had dwindled to roughly 1,600.
At the same time, TFA’s politics moved from the background to the brand. Its public messaging began weighing in more directly on policing, structural racism, gender, and identity.
The more TFA asked people to agree on issues beyond student achievement, the harder it became to sustain the big tent that had once made it so powerful.
The test will be whether Teach For America can once again make its core proposition broad and compelling enough that people with different politics and worldviews can be a part of it.
